title: Preparing data and features
hook: Gaps, text categories, new columns, and rare outcomes. Do it in the right order.
inPlainWords: Features are the columns a model gets to see. Better features usually beat a better algorithm. The order matters: split first, prepare second.

useCase.title: Cancellation data with gaps and a rare outcome
useCase.story: Only 4% of customers cancel. Some ages are missing, "country" is text, and dates are raw timestamps. All of it must be fixed before training.

approaches.name: Drop rows with gaps
approaches.what: Delete rows that have missing values.
approaches.greatWhen: Few gaps and plenty of data.
approaches.avoidWhen: Gaps are common, or not random. People may leave things blank for a reason.

approaches.name: Fill gaps and flag them
approaches.what: Fill in a typical value and add a column saying it was missing.
approaches.greatWhen: Gaps are frequent, or the gap itself carries a clue.
approaches.example: Age is blank, so fill a typical age and set age_missing to yes.

approaches.name: Turn text categories into numbers
approaches.what: Convert labels like country into columns a model can use.
approaches.avoidWhen: Thousands of unique values need special handling.
approaches.example: Country becomes a set of yes or no columns.

approaches.name: Create new features
approaches.what: Combine or reshape raw columns into better clues.
approaches.avoidWhen: You create so many that they mostly add noise.

approaches.name: Put numbers on similar scales
approaches.avoidWhen: Tree models do not need it.
approaches.example: Spend in dollars and visits in counts both scaled.

approaches.name: Handle rare outcomes
approaches.what: Give rare cases more weight, or resample the training data, and judge with measures that reward catching them.
approaches.greatWhen: Rare events like cancellations and fraud.
approaches.avoidWhen: Never alter the exam set. It must look like real life.
approaches.example: Cancellations count ten times more during training.

challenge.question: Only 4% of customers cancel. A model that says "nobody cancels" is 96% accurate. What do you do?

options.why: The model has learned nothing useful. It always guesses "stays".

options.text: Weight the rare cases, judge with catch-rate and false-alarm measures, and leave the exam set untouched
options.why: The model must earn its score on realistic data.
The exam should look like real life, where cancellations are rare.
A sound technique, but you still need the right measures to judge it.

bestCase.title: Split first, fix the training data, add useful features
bestCase.example: days_since_last_visit becomes the strongest clue. Cancellers get more weight in training. The exam set keeps the real 4%, so the final score reflects real life.

worstCase.title: Cleaning before splitting, and rewarding the lazy answer
worstCase.example: You fill gaps using averages from the whole table, including the exam rows, so exam information leaks into training. The model catches nothing yet reports 96% accuracy by always guessing "stays".

route.travelling: Raw row: last visit January 10, age blank, country IN

steps.label: Raw table
steps.goes: Blank ages, text countries, raw dates.

steps.label: Split first
steps.goes: Set the exam rows aside before touching anything.
steps.goesWrong: Everything is cleaned first, then split. Exam information leaks into training.

steps.label: Fix gaps and text
steps.goes: Fill age, flag it as missing, and turn country into columns.

takeaway: Split first, prepare second, and never let a lazy answer earn a good score.
